The RCP is a vertical, centrifugal type pump. The pump is designed to use traditional seals designed to allow continued operation of the pump for a period of at least one week after failure of one of the several stages in order to permit an orderly plant shutdown, without excessive loss of reactor coolant, in the event of the degradation of a second seal stage. The RCP has provisions to prevent motor damage due to overheating by the use of an onboard heat exchanger that is supplied with component cooling water.

Two pressurizer safety valves protect the reactor coolant pressure boundary from excessive pressure during any transients. The pressurizer safety valves provide overpressure protection in accordance with ASME Boiler Pressure and Vessel Code Section III [13]. Discharge lines are routed from the outlet of each pressurizer safety valve to the PCMWT. The pressurizer safety valve sizing analysis will ensure the capability of the SMR-300 design to adequately cope with the most limiting overpressure transients.

The Holtec SMR-300 is comprised of a number of systems that work together to produce electrical energy. When the safe operation of the SMR-300 is challenged, the plant is designed to shut down and enter a long term safe stable condition. The SMR-300 Probabilistic Safety Analysis (PSA) is associated with evaluating the very small possibility that the plant is not able to reach a safe stable condition, and that core damage and potentially a radioactive release occurs. Since not all systems are required to safely shut down the plant, the PSA is focused on those systems that play a role in shutting down the plant and ensuring it reaches a safe stable condition.

The Reactor Coolant Pumps (RCPs) are designed to trip (stop running) in response to a SMR-300 plant trip that actuates the Decay Heat Removal (DHR) function or involves a loss of offsite power which powers the RCPs [8]. Failure of the RCP tripping for DHR actuation is not explicitly modeled in the RCS fault tree analysis since this failure potential (failure to trip automatically represented as a relay failure or RCP breaker failure on two series channels which would be ANDed with each other, which would in turn be ANDed with Operator failing to trip the RCPs) would be orders of magnitude below the PSV failure probability and is screened from consideration. It is also assumed that the initial RCP breaker failure to trip does not prevent the backup operator action to trip the RCPs. This is a reasonable assumption and typical treatment for RCP design and modeling.

The operational procedures for low power and shutdown conditions are described, highlighting the specific actions required to transition the RCS safely from normal to shutdown mode.

The procedures for Level 2 operations, which involve more severe conditions and potential core damage, are detailed. This includes the actions required to mitigate the effects of such events and ensure the reactor remains in a safe condition.
The operator actions required during normal plant operations involving the RCS are detailed, ensuring that operators are well-informed and prepared to handle routine tasks.

During accident conditions the RCPs are not required to remain functional [6]. The only safety functions of the RCPs are to provide adequate pump coast down to ensure reactor coolant continues to flow for a short time after pump trip and to maintain the RCPB.

The PSVs would remain closed during accident conditions unless RCS pressure exceeds their opening setpoint. In that case, the PSVs would be expected to open to lower RCS pressure and subsequently reclose when RCS pressure is again below the PSV opening setpoint to maintain the RCPB.

G7. THE FLEX DOUBLER FUNCTION TAKES INPUT OF A COUNT RATE FROM ONE OF THE SOURCE RANGE CHANNELS. THE CALCULATION CALCULATES A RUNNING AVERAGE OF THE PREVIOUS MINUTE, AS WELL AS THE PREVIOUS NINE MINUTE INTERVAL. IF THE MOST RECENT INTERVAL IS GREATER THAN TWO TIMES ANY OF THE PREVIOUS NINE ONE MINUTE INTERVALS, THE OUTPUT IS TRUE.

10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 1 [24]: GDC 1 requires the RAB, which is important to safety, to be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of its safety function, a quality assurance program be established and implemented, and that sufficient and appropriate records be maintained.

10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 2 [24] and 10CFR50 Appendix S [25]: GDC 2 [24] and Appendix S [25] require the RAB, which is important to safety, to be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, such as earthquakes, without loss of capability to perform their safety functions.
RAB shall provide sufficient number of sumps for the collection of equipment and floor drains.

The materials used shall meet the applicable requirements of American Concrete Institute (ACI) 349 [13] for concrete structures and American Institute of Steel Construction (AISC) N690 [14] for steel structures, including any standards referenced therein.
The interior finish and decorative materials used for the RAB shall meet the applicable requirements of IBC [15] or relevant specification produced by Holtec International.

The RAB structural design and systems shall be standardized to the extent possible. This includes structural details and support for piping, electrical raceway, and HVAC ductwork, as well as for purchased equipment.

The RAB design shall accommodate and facilitate the selected construction schedule. System completion, pre-operational and startup testing must be considered in the formulation of the construction schedule.
The RAB design shall permit preassembly and installation of large modules. The selection of scope and design of modules must be evaluated in conjunction with the construction sequence.

In the RAB, space must be allocated adjacent to the structures for installation of temporary elevators to handle peak manpower requirements during construction. Permanent plant elevators should be designed and installed early and should be capable of heavy-duty operation during the construction phase, EPRI URD, Chapter 6, Section 4.12.2.1 [47].
Site construction requirements shall be developed during the detailed design.

Structural members shall be designed with provisions like anchor bolts, embedment plates etc. for supporting components. The design and analysis of anchors (steel embedment) used for components and structural supports on concrete structures shall be in accordance with applicable guidelines in Appendix D to ACI 349 [3], as supplemented by RG 1.199 [30].

Design in concrete attachments shall be avoided as a design basis but may be used as design alternatives to embedment plates for supports that require relocation during construction after the concrete is cast.
The local effect of the attachment loads as well as the effect on the gross structure must be considered in the design.
8.13.4. Structural steel columns shall be used for building designs in lieu of free-standing concrete columns, where technically feasible.

8.13.7. Concrete walls shall be sized to facilitate the use of embedded plates to relieve rebar congestion.
8.13.8. Concrete walls shall line up with one another between floor levels, where possible.

8.14.2. The RAB shall provide access to the personnel access hatch (personnel access to the containment during shutdown).
8.14.3. The RAB shall provide access to all containment penetrations and associated isolation valves.

8.14.4. The RAB shall provide overhead door access for HI-TRAC movement from roadways. The overhead door shall be designed to minimize the contamination from the radiologically controlled area to outside.
8.14.5. The RAB design shall conform to system interfacing requirements between the RAB area and neighboring areas as defined within individual system requirements.
8.14.6. The RAB design shall accommodate leakage detection systems for AR and PCMWT, as applicable.

8.15.2. Inspection and testing of steel structures shall be guided by those in AISC N690 [14].

Provision shall also be made for three active observers and assistants in the main controlling area of the MCR: • One from the NRC; • One to the Plant Owner's management; • One to handle communications.

In-plant noise levels must not exceed 90 dBA for an 8-h exposure. Plant perimeter noise levels must not exceed 65 dBA during the day and 55 dBA during the night, EPRI URD, Chapter 1, Appendix C, Annex A [47].

All control stations which are continuously manned on a routine basis, e.g., the MCR, the technical support center, and the emergency operations facility, shall have an ambient noise level no greater than 60 dBA from installed equipment in the immediate neighborhood of the control station and plant equipment which may operate for long periods. This limit shall be met for all normal or emergency HVAC system lineups in all areas of those control stations where communication between operators is necessary.

All control stations which may be continuously manned for substantial periods of time, e.g., the MCR, the technical support center, and the emergency operations facility, shall be provided with carpeting and sound absorbing walls and ceilings. These materials shall be selected for fire resistance, ease of upkeep, durability, freedom from generation of static electricity, and appearance in addition to their sound absorption.

The MCR shall have at least two independent exits which can be used in case the MCR must be evacuated. The remote shutdown station(s) shall be accessible to the operators from either exit without the use of security devices such as keys or key cards and without electric power.

A restroom adequate for both men and women shall be provided. Kitchen facilities with provisions for food preparation shall be provided (e.g., an oven, hot water, drinking water, and refrigeration). These facilities shall not be shared with areas outside the MCR.
The arrangement of the workstations in the MCR shall facilitate direct communication between the operators at the workstations. This includes the ability for direct conversation and visual contact.
Radiation protection as applicable to RAB for plant, personnel, public and environment shall comply with the requirements established in the SMR-160 Design Standard for Radiation Protection [3].

The RAB design shall include provisions for handling and processing personnel to control contamination and radiation exposure (minimize or eliminate the need for plant personnel to enter areas greater than 100 mrem/hr for routine operation). Additionally, radiation monitoring will be placed in all discharge lines with an interlock/permissive to automatically isolate any permitted liquid or gaseous release should the release allowance criteria be exceeded.
Security and radiological control points shall be sized to accommodate personnel with minimum delay and shall be sized based on major maintenance operations or normal operations, whichever controls.

The MCR wall, ceiling, and floor materials and thickness shall be designed such that operators as well as other plant personnel are protected from radiation sources associated with normal plant operation and postulated initiating events (PIE).
Structures designed to manage radioactive waste shall comply with the guidance provided in Regulatory Guide 1.143 [27].

Following the guidance of Regulatory Guide 4.21 [53], the design features shall be provided to minimize contamination of the facility and environment, facilitate decommissioning and minimize the generation of radioactive material to comply with the 10 CFR 20.1406 [39]. Design features to reduce accumulation of radioactive material in components of systems used to process resin and sludges should reflect specific considerations given in Section C.2.(h) of RG 8.8 [54].
Concrete radiation shields shall be designed in accordance with Regulatory Guide 1.69 [3].

Streaming of radiation into accessible areas through penetrations for pipes, ducts, and other shield discontinuities is reduced by using layouts that prevent alignment with the radiation source, placing penetrations above head height to reduce personnel exposures, and using shadow shields to attenuate radiation streaming. Shield wall penetrations shall be sufficiently compensated to comply with the associated radiation zone map dose rates for normally accessible areas.

GDC 3 requires the RAB to be designed and located to minimize the probability and effect of fires and explosions.

GDC 4 requires the RAB to be appropriately protected against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids, that may result from equipment failures and from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit.

GDC 60 requires that the nuclear power unit design include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents and to handle radioactive solid waste produced during normal reactor operation, including anticipated operational occurrences.

The RAB is designed to perform the following safety functions: Provide protection and separation for the Seismic Category I structures, and mechanical and electrical equipment located outside the Containment Structure (CS); Class 1E Battery Rooms and associated equipment Containment Penetrations/Accessways Safety-related Instrumentation and Control (I&C) Provide control room with provisions for plant operators to monitor and operate the plant during normal conditions and safely shutdown the plant following a design basis accident.

The RAB is designed to perform the following non-safety functions: House systems, components, and structures critical for the normal operation/shutdown of the plant such as RHR, CVC, SFC, radwaste systems and CCW. Provide provisions to support spent fuel removal to interim dry storage. Provide provisions to support new fuel receipt and storage. Provide HVAC for all the components and structures of the RAB and containment purging. Provide radiation protection for plant personnel from radioactive components and minimization of contamination and radioactive waste generation, by incorporating the following design features to ensure compliance with applicable regulations such as 10 CFR 20.1101 [38] and 10 CFR 20.1406 [39] correspondingly: Radiation zoning and access control, Remotely operated Process Instrumentation and Controls, Isolation and decontamination of substantial radiation sources, Minimization of accumulation of radioactive materials in Resin and Sludge Treatment Systems etc. Provide suitable environments for personnel and equipment during all phases of plant operation. Provide adequate laydown space to facilitate inspection, testing, and maintenance of structures, systems, and components located within the RAB. Provide cooling to all the penetrations into RAB in excess of 500°F to ensure no long- term concrete degradation. Control, collect, process, handle, store, segregate and dispose of radwaste. Process and dispose of steam generator blowdown if significant radioactivity is detected. Degas reactor coolant in conjunction with the Chemical and Volume Control System (CVC). Transport processed gases to the monitored release point.
Provide the means for receiving, inspecting and storing the new fuel assemblies.
Provide the means for transferring new fuel assemblies (from the RAB) into the transfer cask which is then transported into the CS for loading into the reactor core.
Provide a dry storage preparation area where spent fuel (in the transfer cask) is prepared for loading into dry storage casks outside the RAB.
Protect spent fuel assemblies (in the transfer cask), the new fuel assemblies, and radioactive systems from external events such as tornadoes and tornado generated missiles.
Prevent the release of airborne radioactivity following any postulated design basis accident (DBA) from exceeding site boundary radiation levels.
Provide a Hot Equipment Storage Area to house equipment used to perform access operations in the CS via the equipment hatch through the RAB.
To collect and accumulate a sufficient amount of radioactive waste prior to its transfer to another facility.
To collect and accumulate a sufficient amount of radioactive waste prior to its disposal.
To provide long-term storage of radioactive waste when a suitable disposal facility is lacking.

A Radiologically Controlled Area (RCA) associated with higher dose rates should be kept as small as reasonably achievable consistent with accessibility for accomplishing the services that must be performed in those areas, including equipment laydown requirements. RCA where plant personnel spend substantial time should be designed to the lowest practical dose rates.

Appropriate station layout and design features should be provided to reduce the potential doses to personnel who must operate, service, or inspect RAB instrumentation and controls. Where it is impracticable to provide permanent shielding for individual components that constitute substantial radiation sources, the exposure of maintenance personnel shall be reduced by providing as much distance as practicable between the serviceable components and the substantial radiation sources in the area and through the use of "reach rods" or remotely operated valves or controls.

Radioactive system components should be located separately from "clean" components as much as practical. Individual components of a radioactive system should be located in separate shielded compartments with short piping runs between components. Where appropriate, shielded valve galleries are employed to allow system operation while shielding operators from high radiation components.

Whenever possible, pipes with radioactive fluids shall be routed through pipe chases or shielded areas, and away from pipes for "clean" services. If pipes with radioactive fluids are routed near clean service pipes, provisions for isolation and draining of the radioactive pipes should be provided. Piping is designed to minimize "dead legs" and low points.

This access shall not disrupt the actions of the operating team in the main controlling area of the MCR unless it is necessary for efficient communication.

Specifically, in addition to adequate space in the main controlling area for visiting plant staff, space for consultation shall be provided outside the main controlling area and access to that space shall not require passage through the main controlling area.

Access by NRC inspectors and provisions for them to communicate with their headquarters, with the shift supervisor, or with the Plant Owner management without disrupting MCR activities;

The Reactor Auxiliary Building is a multi-story structure which houses safety-related and non-safety-related systems, structures, and components for the SMR-300 plant. This design specification report provides information on codes and standards, regulatory requirements, general requirements, safety and non-safety related functions, design conditions, environmental conditions, and load combinations for the Reactor Auxiliary Building.

This access shall not disrupt the actions of the operating team in the main controlling area of the MCR unless it is necessary for efficient communication.

Specifically, in addition to adequate space in the main controlling area for visiting plant staff, space for consultation shall be provided outside the main controlling area and access to that space shall not require passage through the main controlling area.

The location, arrangement, and equipment in the MCR shall facilitate the necessary interaction between the operators in the MCR and other personnel, even though these contacts do not appear explicitly in the tasks assigned to the operators in the MCR. The MCR design shall identify all such interactions or contacts which have been considered in the design basis. The objective of the MCR arrangement shall be to limit the contacts of these non-operating personnel so that normally they do not distract the operators at the controls in the main controlling area of the MCR. In particular, routine contacts with the shift supervisor, the shift supervisor's clerk, the RO assigned to switching and tagging, or the shift technical advisor shall not require personnel to pass through the main controlling area of the MCR. Some specific items which shall be included are the following:
Access by NRC inspectors and provisions for them to communicate with their headquarters, with the shift supervisor, or with the Plant Owner management without disrupting MCR activities;

The layout of the MCR shall include an area designated as an operator relief area. This area should be adjacent to the kitchen and restroom facilities as well as being immediately accessible to the main controlling area of the MCR. The relief area shall be of sufficient size to allow an operator to relax and engage in limited physical activity.

The layout of the MCR shall specifically provide for the operations involved in shift turnover. In particular, a location where the personnel for a shift may meet without disturbing the activities in the main part of the MCR shall be provided. This area may be combined with operators' relief area (see Section 4.9.1.4 of the URD [47]).

All control stations which are continuously manned on a routine basis, e.g., the MCR, the technical support center, and the emergency operations facility, shall have an ambient noise level no greater than 60 dBA from installed equipment in the immediate neighborhood of the control station and plant equipment which may operate for long periods. This limit shall be met for all normal or emergency HVAC system lineups in all areas of those control stations where communication between operators is necessary.

All control stations which may be continuously manned for substantial periods of time, e.g., the MCR, the technical support center, and the emergency operations facility, shall be provided with carpeting and sound absorbing walls and ceilings. These materials shall be selected for fire resistance, ease of upkeep, durability, freedom from generation of static electricity, and appearance in addition to their sound absorption.

The MCR shall have at least two independent exits which can be used in case the MCR must be evacuated. The remote shutdown station(s) shall be accessible to the operators from either exit without the use of security devices such as keys or key cards and without electric power.

A restroom adequate for both men and women shall be provided. Kitchen facilities with provisions for food preparation shall be provided (e.g., an oven, hot water, drinking water, and refrigeration). These facilities shall not be shared with areas outside the MCR.

entry.section_title: 10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 2 [24] and 10CFR50 Appendix S [25]
entry.text: GDC 2 [24] and Appendix S [25] require the RAB, which is important to safety, to be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, such as earthquakes, without loss of capability to perform their safety functions.
GDC 3 requires the RAB to be designed and located to minimize the probability and effect of fires and explosions.

GDC 4 requires the RAB to be appropriately protected against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids, that may result from equipment failures and from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit.

GDC 60 requires that the nuclear power unit design include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents and to handle radioactive solid waste produced during normal reactor operation, including anticipated operational occurrences.

The RAB is designed to perform the following safety functions: Provide protection and separation for the Seismic Category I structures, and mechanical and electrical equipment located outside the Containment Structure (CS); Class 1E Battery Rooms and associated equipment Containment Penetrations/Accessways Safety-related Instrumentation and Control (I&C) Provide control room with provisions for plant operators to monitor and operate the plant during normal conditions and safely shutdown the plant following a design basis accident.

The RAB is designed to perform the following non-safety functions: House systems, components, and structures critical for the normal operation/shutdown of the plant such as RHR, CVC, SFC, radwaste systems and CCW. Provide provisions to support spent fuel removal to interim dry storage. Provide provisions to support new fuel receipt and storage. Provide HVAC for all the components and structures of the RAB and containment purging. Provide radiation protection for plant personnel from radioactive components and minimization of contamination and radioactive waste generation, by incorporating the following design features to ensure compliance with applicable regulations such as 10 CFR 20.1101 [38] and 10 CFR 20.1406 [39] correspondingly: Radiation zoning and access control, Remotely operated Process Instrumentation and Controls, Isolation and decontamination of substantial radiation sources, Minimization of accumulation of radioactive materials in Resin and Sludge Treatment Systems etc. Provide suitable environments for personnel and equipment during all phases of plant operation. Provide adequate laydown space to facilitate inspection, testing, and maintenance of structures, systems, and components located within the RAB. Provide cooling to all the penetrations into RAB in excess of 500°F to ensure no long- term concrete degradation. Control, collect, process, handle, store, segregate and dispose of radwaste. Process and dispose of steam generator blowdown if significant radioactivity is detected. Degas reactor coolant in conjunction with the Chemical and Volume Control System (CVC). Transport processed gases to the monitored release point.

Heater SCC is capable of both modulating and on/off control. This enables swapping heater group designation as proportional, backup or steady state from the MCR without shutting down. Proportional control selected will enable manual setpoint control. The backup control selection enables the pop and clamp commands to control the heater group based on the manually set backup setpoint. The manual control selection places the heater group in manual direct control and is used for turning heaters off, as for outages, and for steady-state operation. Each of these mode selections are done manually from the pressure control HFE screen. A clamp demand is provided to prevent heaters starting or operating with insufficient coverage.

Each heater group is equipped with a standard component control that will accommodate its operation as a steady state (always on during normal operation), a proportional (partially on proportional to how much pressurizer pressure has fallen below its setpoint) operation, or a backup (fully on only when pressurizer pressure is significantly below its setpoint) operation. This capability is described and defined in Appendix J. Heater mode selection is done via a screen at the operational visual display unit (O-VDU) using buttons and logic described visually by Figure 7-1. The controls depicted in Figure 7-1 for heater group A are the same for heater groups B, C and D.

entry.section_title: Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System
entry.text: The proportional heater receives a setpoint from the operator based on normal operating pressure and proportional heater offset (see Figure 7-2). This is the default mode of operation when the heaters are in manual setpoint control. At normal operating pressure, the proportional heater has minimal voltage applied. As pressure falls below the setpoint, the proportional heater increases in power to a maximum at some margin below the setpoint. The applied voltage between these two points is linear. This allows for prolonged operating life of the proportional heater and backup heaters by minimizing heater power cycles from minor transients and losses to ambient. If a heater fails and a deviation alarm is issued, it additionally transfers its mode of operation to that of a backup heater.

entry.section_title: Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System
entry.text: The heater banks identified as backup heaters turn on when pressure falls to a manually set pressure significantly below the normal operating pressure. This will provide additional heater input to raise pressure back to normal operating pressure in case a transient exceeds the capacity of proportional and steady state heaters.

entry.section_title: Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System
entry.text: The spray control valves are pressure control valves which open to permit subcooled spray into the PZR steam space to lower pressure through condensation. The spray valve will operate to maintain normal operating pressure at the manual setpoint (see Figure 7-2), opening as pressure rises and shutting as it decreases. Further detail regarding the control of the spray valve is found in Appendix J.

Basis for Control: The spray line isolation valves are for isolating flow through a faulty spray control valve and for isolating a LOCA in the associated spray line from the RPV and the PZR. They are manually controlled from the MCR. They will automatically shut in the event of a failure of the associated spray control valve.

The RCS uses forced flow from startup to shut down to provide core cooling and is achieved by running two RCPs. The RCPs are controlled manually from the MCR and are prevented from starting without adequate system pressure to provide NPSH. They are automatically tripped from a DHR actuation signal. Appendix J contains further details regarding the control scheme for the RCPs.

The RPV seals are connected to lines that lead to a temperature sensor. In case the primary seal fails, the temperature sensor will detect the high-temperature leak off from the failed seal. This prompts the operators to shift to the secondary seal. By shutting the primary leak off isolation valve and opening the secondary. If further leakage is detected, the operator will assess for shutdown and repairs rather than allow seal leakage to spill over to the RPV exterior.

entry.text: The PDRHR and SDRHR are designed to reject decay heat from the RCS during all initiating events with the reactor coolant pressure boundary intact, where the normal heat rejection path is assumed to be lost. The PDRHR system is individually capable of removing 100% of the plant's decay heat indefinitely. The PDRHR rejects its heat to the Passive Core Makeup Water Tank (PCMWT) inside containment, while the SDRHR rejects its heat to the AR outside containment.

The PDHR and SDHR are designed to remove decay heat from the RCS when normal cooling is not available. The ADS and the PCMWS are designed to provide core cooling for the complete range of loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA) required to be considered by nuclear regulations. The ADS is a staged energy relieving system for the primary circuit, separate from the ASME Boiler & Pressure Vessel Code safety relief valves. All makeup water required for LOCA events is inside containment, such that the containment can be fully isolated to prevent release of radioactivity.

entry.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entry.text: GEH and its partners are developing a design and a SAR to satisfy universal, and initially Canadian nuclear regulations, as needed to construct and license an FOAK reactor. The design includes certain basic features that will challenge regulations both in Canada, and in competent nuclear design regions around the world, given different cultures, experiences, insights and OPEX in those regions. Certain fundamental elements of the design introduce first-of-a-kind components, operations and technologies not previously developed, tested, or proven for use in nuclear reactor applications, and these elements introduce significant risks and challenges to the concept as currently envisioned. The design relies on a single Isolation Condenser System to perform numerous crucial safety functions, with no capability to ensure a safely cooled and shutdown reactor in case that ICS fails for any reason, foreseeable or not. The Fukushima accident is still fresh in the minds and memories of the world, where the unit-1 reactor core melted after the ICS did not perform as expected. GEH has promised that they have learned from this accident and improved the ICS - but have eliminated all other BWR safety systems in pursuit of cost reduction.

entry.section_title: KEY RISKS, Challenges, Potential Fatal Flaws
entry.text: GEH describes the BWRX-300 as requiring no core injection for LOCA mitigation, while noting the design includes high pressure injection via the fine motion control drive system. The BWRX-300 Emergency Core Cooling System relies entirely on the ICS to supply water and handle over pressure with fail safe (closed) double isolation valves integrated to reactor vessel for steam, feed, ICS exit and ICS return pipes.

entry.section_title: Lack of Independence for Shut Down System (SDS)
entry.text: The BWRX-300 control blades are used for power control, fuel reactivity management and power shaping, and for shutdown, startup, and scram. As such, the basic design does not include a second independent means to shut down the reactor, as expected and required by many competent regulators. While the design includes a Boron Injection System (BIS), this system will be credited to add negative reactivity but has no dedicated independent instrumentation or actuation logic and is not automated. Accordingly, it is not a credited shut down system according to today's interpreted regulations in the US, Canada, the UK, and other internationally regulated nuclear domains. Furthermore, it is not obvious how the plant can achieve assured safe shutdown for seven days without operator actions as the developer claims, as the BIS included in the plant design for an Anticipated Transient Without Scram (ATWS) is not automated and requires operator actions to actuate if or when needed. The FOIAK application in Canada will need to overcome the matter that Canadian regulations plainly require two independent shutdown systems.

entry.section_title: Lack of Independence for Shut Down System (SDS)
entry.text: CANDU power plants have a positive void coefficient of reactivity. As a result, power can increase rapidly following postulated LOCA. This design characteristic is the primary driver for having two shutdown systems in current CANDUs. In addition, CANDU accident analysis for LOCA events defines performance requirements for key reactivity control measures (e.g., shutdown system speed and reactivity depth). Like most LWRs, the BWRX-300 has a negative void coefficient of reactivity, whereby void formations decrease reactivity and tend to shut LWRs down. For these LWRs, many of the traditional safety analysis issues in CANDU LOCA do not exhibit power excursions. entry.section_title: Figure 3-1: The Holtec SMR-300 in perspective view
entry.text: The Holtec SMR-300 plant has no penetrations in the lower 2/3rd of the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV). An Annular Reservoir (AR) containing over one million gallons of water surrounds the containment vessel which is enclosed by the Containment Enclosure Structure (CES). This reservoir can provide cooling to the containment for greater than 90 days in the event of a loss of cooling accident, followed by a transition to indefinite air cooling; no operator action is necessary to achieve this - the plant is walk-away safe. The above-grade steel Containment Structure (CS) serves as both a containment and a large passive heat exchanger to reject decay heat through the containment wall into the annular reservoir. The deeply embedded CS is protected from aircraft and missile impact by the thick CES, with the plant's nuclear commodities - reactor, core and spent fuel pool - located below grade. The CES, characterized by a deep below-ground foundation with a cylindrical cross section assembled from CSSM modules is configured expressly to withstand impulsive and impactive loads.

entry.section_title: Figure 3-1: The Holtec SMR-300 in perspective view
entry.text: The Holtec SMR-300 design specification includes evaluation of the highest earthquake and most severe environmental phenomena loads, yielding an adaptable bounding standard plant design which will envelope most US and global sites. This approach fixes the plant's anatomy during the design phase, with enough additional margin embedded in each critical area to preclude the need for gross site-specific design changes. Site conditions and utility functional requirements may inform the electric power output, but not the standard plant design. The energy allocated to electric power and process-heat may be adjusted to suit local needs, lending SMR-300 plants to broad load-following capabilities. Coupled with an energy storage system, the Holtec SMR-300 can further enhance grid stability and energy efficiencies.

entry.section_title: Figure 3-1: The Holtec SMR-300 in perspective view
entry.text: The CES and surrounding seismic category 1 structures (the most resilient type, required to assure nuclear safety in a worst case earthquake) are designed to prevent damage to any components of the nuclear steam supply system (NSSS) or any radiological release to the atmosphere in the event of a design basis earthquake, aircraft impact or any other external hazards. SMR-300 core components and reactor internals are readily removable for refueling, inspection, maintenance or change-out without disassembly of the reactor coolant system (RCS), or disconnection from its principal safety systems. The steam generator allows easy access for eddy current inspections as performed in the current US PWR fleet, and convenient in-service inspection.

entry.text: The Holtec SMR-300 plant has no penetrations in the lower 2/3rd of the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV). An Annular Reservoir (AR) containing over one million gallons of water surrounds the containment vessel which is enclosed by the Containment Enclosure Structure (CES). This reservoir can provide cooling to the containment for greater than 90 days in the event of a loss of cooling accident, followed by a transition to indefinite air cooling; no operator action is necessary to achieve this - the plant is walk-away safe. The above-grade steel Containment Structure (CS) serves as both a containment and a large passive heat exchanger to reject decay heat through the containment wall into the annular reservoir. The deeply embedded CS is protected from aircraft and missile impact by the thick CES, with the plant's nuclear commodities - reactor, core and spent fuel pool - located below grade. The CES, characterized by a deep below-ground foundation with a cylindrical cross section assembled from CSSM modules is configured expressly to withstand impulsive and impactive loads.

entry.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entry.text: GEH and its partners are developing a design and a SAR to satisfy universal, and initially Canadian nuclear regulations, as needed to construct and license an FOAK reactor. The design includes certain basic features that will challenge regulations both in Canada, and in competent nuclear design regions around the world, given different cultures, experiences, insights and OPEX in those regions. Certain fundamental elements of the design introduce first-of-a-kind components, operations and technologies not previously developed, tested, or proven for use in nuclear reactor applications, and these elements introduce significant risks and challenges to the concept as currently envisioned. The design relies on a single Isolation Condenser System to perform numerous crucial safety functions, with no capability to ensure a safely cooled and shutdown reactor in case that ICS fails for any reason, foreseeable or not. The Fukushima accident is still fresh in the minds and memories of the world, where the unit-1 reactor core melted after the ICS did not perform as expected. GEH has promised that they have learned from this accident and improved the ICS - but have eliminated all other BWR safety systems in pursuit of cost reduction.

The power plant produces clean super-heated steam ideal for both electricity generation and process heat applications. The plant is offered in both a single unit and a standard dual-unit configuration, the latter to optimize construction and operating costs, and to eliminate single-shaft failure risk to the production of thermal and electric power. The object of this approach is to make sure that all plants, no matter where deployed, shall be virtually identical and standardized, helping minimize construction time and cost and facilitating the use of standard plant procedures.

entry.text: Vibration: Vibration of slender parts such as tubes in feedwater heaters, control condensers, steam generators, moisture separator reheaters, auxiliary feed exchangers, surface rod extensions, and piping runs has been a persistent operating problem in nuclear plants. In the Holtec SMR-300, this ubiquitous problem is systematically solved by requiring that the fundamental natural frequency of the part be at least two times the highest frequency of the excitation source. In heat exchangers, principal excitation sources are fluid elastic coupling and turbulent buffeting. Piping runs are vulnerable to the harmonics associated with earthquakes.

This report documents one of several mechanical analyses performed for the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV), as defined in Reference [1], for the SMR-300. The included analyses are performed to demonstrate that the sizing of the design is structurally adequate to meet the design requirements and acceptance criteria set forth by 10 CFR 50 with endorsements to the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel code. This, and other analyses, will ensure all aspects of the RPV design assembly, will satisfy all structural and functional requirements. This report focuses on the RPV heads, shells and nozzles sizing when subjected to Design Pressure, Design Temperature, Test Pressure, and estimated piping loads only. A minimum thickness calculation is also performed. Accordingly, only primary stress for these conditions was evaluated. Safety factors were computed, and recommendations are provided to remedy potential unsatisfactory conditions. The analysis focuses on the RPV geometry defined in Reference [1], and does not consider the geometry of any interfacing components. In addition to regulatory requirements, the SMR-300 RPV must satisfy the criteria specified in the Owners (i.e. Holtec International, as defined by ASME Section III, Division 1, Subsection NCA) (Reference [3]), certified RPV ASME Design Specification. The RPV ASME Design Specification classifies the RPV as a Division 1, Class 1 item (per NCA-2100), which requires the design and analysis to be completed in accordance with the rules contained in ASME Section III, Division 1, Subsection NB (Reference [4]). The RPV ASME Design Specification is not currently available for this report. The scope of this report is therefore limited to initial superimposed loads, Design Pressure and Design Temperature loadings, and Hydrostatic testing load conditions. After the ASME Design Specification is completed, future analyses will be performed to show that the RPV satisfies all the criteria contained within the ASME Design Specification including all load combinations for ASME Service Levels A, B, C, and D. Stresses from superimposed mechanical loads on the RPV due to interactions with interfacing components such as the Control Rod Drive Mechanisms and Reactor Vessel Internals are not included in this report. Additionally, triaxial stress and comparison to the ASME limits were not included in this report.

Two pressurizer safety valves protect the reactor coolant pressure boundary from excessive pressure during any transients. Reactor coolant piping is designed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section III [8]. The reactor coolant piping maintains the reactor coolant pressure boundary and is designed to withstand the maximum RCS pressure and temperature under all expected modes of plant operation and anticipated operational occurrences. Seamless piping is used to avoid in-service inspection of longitudinal piping welds. The piping material for the hot legs and cold legs shall be carbon steel with stainless steel cladding. All other piping shall be stainless steel.

During this transition the Residual Heat Removal System is in operation to control RCS temperature and provides low temperature overpressure protection (LTOP). Either RHHR or CVC is used to fill the RCS. Once the RCS is water solid, the operators energize the pressurizer heaters and discharge coolant via CVC letdown to draw a bubble in the Pressurizer to establish RCS pressure control. Operators establish pressure control below brittle fracture prevention limits (BFPL) and LTOP setpoints. Once system pressure is greater than NPSHR, the RCPs can begin circulating water in the RCS. The RCPs provide the heat input to raise RCS temperature. RCPs also provide heat for spray flow to allow mixing and pressure control in the pressurizer, CVC may be used to provide auxiliary spray flow as necessary prior to starting RCPs. Primary

To prevent a common failure and assure protection for pipe breaks, missiles, and fires, safety-related valves and components will meet the grouping and separation requirements described in section 4.2.4.

Redundant valves in series assure isolation of the RCS to maintain the reactor coolant pressure boundary and ensure an inadvertent actuation of a valve will not result in a LOCA. The RPV head vent forms the high point for the RPV and are designed with redundant valves in series to assure isolation in case an open vent valve cannot be closed. The failure mode and effects analysis in Appendix A provide a summary of the system response to a single failure of components with a safety function.

The equipment arrangement inside containment will be designed to permit periodic inspection and testing. Sufficient space will be provided for
Provisions for disassembly and inspection of RCP components, including motors and seals, are accounted for in containment layout and will be developed in detail after pump selection.

The Leak Detection System will be developed for detecting and monitoring RCS leakage. Leak-Before-Break methodology and associated in-service inspection criterion leakage detection will be applied to portions of the RCS piping to minimize the probability of a pipe rupture.

System pressure tests (leakage and hydrostatic) will be performed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15]. The charging pump in the Chemical and Volume Control System can be used for the system leakage test at the RCS pressure corresponding to 100% rated reactor power, in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15] Article IWB-5000 for system pressure tests.

The pressurizer safety valves will be tested and qualified (10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(i)(x) for TMI Action Plan Item II.D.1 [16]) by the EPRI Test Program [17]. The LTOP relief valve that is part of the RHR has a set pressure less than the full RCS design pressure, therefore, this relief valve is excluded from the EPRI Test Program and will be covered by the test program that will be developed later.

The RCS provides a flow path for reactor coolant to remove heat from the reactor core, which supports maintaining the fuel condition within the operating bounds. Reactor coolant is transported through the RCS to transfer heat from the fuel to the balance of plant systems via the steam generator during Power Operation as well as in the Hot Standby and Safe Shutdown modes (when the reactor is subcritical). RCS transfers the core decay heat to the RHR system during the subsequent phases of Safe Shutdown, Cold Shutdown, and Refueling modes. During a design basis accident where the reactor coolant pressure boundary remains intact, the RCS transfers core decay heat from the fuel to the PCMWT via the Primary Decay Heat Removal System (PDH) and to the SGE via the Secondary Decay Heat Removal System (SDH). During design basis accidents where the reactor coolant pressure boundary fails, such as a loss of coolant accident (LOCA), connections at the reactor pressure vessel provide for direct safety injection of coolant to meet emergency core cooling requirements. During a loss of RCPs, the flywheel provides continued flow for a short period ensuring coast down requirements are met.

To ensure operational limits are not exceeded. The pressurizer maintains the system pressure during operation and limits pressure transients by establishing a saturated vapor-liquid interface (i.e., steam bubble). The pressurizer is sized to accommodate volume changes in the reactor coolant during a reduction or increase of plant load during power operations.

Two pressurizer safety valves protect the reactor coolant pressure boundary from excessive pressure during any transients. The pressurizer safety valves provide overpressure protection in accordance with ASME Boiler Pressure Vessel Code Section III [8]. The pressurizer safety valve sizing analysis will ensure the capability of the SMR-300 design to adequately cope with the most limiting overpressure transients.

Reactor coolant piping is designed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section III [8]. The reactor coolant piping maintains the reactor coolant pressure boundary and is designed to withstand the maximum RCS pressure and temperature under all expected modes of plant operation and anticipated operational occurrences. Seamless piping is used to avoid in-service inspection of longitudinal piping welds. The piping material for the hot legs and cold legs shall be carbon steel with stainless steel cladding. All other piping shall be stainless steel.

The application of Leak-Before-Break (LBB) analysis and criteria to portions of the RCS piping design of high energy piping systems is being developed. Using the Leak-Before-Break methodology approved by the NRC and other design considerations can justify a design basis that eliminates jet impingement shields and pipe whip restraints. This methodology requires the ability to detect leaks from cracks smaller than a critical flaw size.

entry.section_title: System Design Description for the Reactor Coolant System
entry.text: The external support for the RPV will be trunnions to the surrounding concrete walls and a lateral restraint at the bottom of the RPV cavity to help withstand seismic events.

The tube side of the SGE is designed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code [8]. The straight OTSG tubes provide easy access for in-service inspection and tube plugging as needed. The OTSG is designed for rated performance with a percentage of the tubes plugged.

The PSS employs 2oo4 voting logic, where any two of the four inputs being true, causes the output to be true. The logic includes the capability to bypass individual channels for maintenance or troubleshooting. Instrument channels are compared to setpoints, and a bistable output is provided that is true when the setpoint is exceeded and false when it is back to normal.

The actuation logic for RT and ESF functions uses a standard set of logic (Figure 4-1). Each actuation logic function is initiated automatically by some specific set of logic for that function and can also be manually initiated by the operator. Once initiated the function is latched at the division level, a manual reset is provided for the operators to reset the function once allowed.

entry.section_title: Reactor Trip and Engineered Safety Features Control Description
entry.text: The PSS employs a two-division design, where either division can initiate an RT or ESF function independent of the other. Each division receives two instrument inputs (U/X for Division A, and Y/Z for Division B) and performs the necessary bistable logic for those inputs. The bistable outputs are then shared to the other division through Data Links so that each division can perform two out of four (2oo4) voting independently. The results of this 2oo4 voting are used in logic for RT and ESF actuation. The PSS employs 2oo4 voting logic, where any two of the four inputs being true, causes the output to be true. The logic includes the capability to bypass individual channels for maintenance or troubleshooting. Instrument channels are compared to setpoints, and a bistable output is provided that is true when the setpoint is exceeded and false when it is back to normal.

entry.section_title: Reactor Trip and Engineered Safety Features Control Description
entry.text: The actuation logic for RT and ESF functions uses a standard set of logic (Figure 4-1). Each actuation logic function is initiated automatically by some specific set of logic for that function and can also be manually initiated by the operator. Once initiated the function is latched at the division level, a manual reset is provided for the operators to reset the function once allowed. Divisional manual initiation can be accomplished from either division of the PSS or from the PCS, and this initiation causes both divisions to actuate (Figure 4-1). Channelized manual initiation require two concurrent initiations (2oo2) from a division or from the PCS to help prevent a spurious actuation (Figure 4-2), and this initiation causes four channels to actuate. Manual reset can also be accomplished from either division of the PSS or from the PCS, and the reset causes both divisions to reset. The reset has a permissive that only allows it to be reset once the division senses that it can be reset. This prevents the other division or PCS from inadvertently resetting the actuation function.

The PSS monitors plant parameters to provide protective action, including Engineered Safety Features actuations, to prevent safety limits from being exceeded. The basis for the parameters and setpoints monitored are included in the SMR-300 Plant Safety System Logic Basis [2]. The PSS initiates an ESF Actuation when required by actuating an ESF component (a valve or breaker) to its safe state. Separate ESF components are provided for each division of the PSS and are configured to meet single failure criteria. Appendix B contains a summary table of all ESF actuations, the components actuated, and the ESF reset permissive signal, explaining which status feedback of the device is used for the permissive signal and how the logic to monitor the necessary plant parameters and initiate an ESF actuation is implemented.

The PSS monitors plant parameters and provides interlocks to ensure systems are aligned to support protective action, including Engineered Safety Features actuations, to prevent safety limits from being exceeded. The basis for the parameters and setpoints monitored are included in the SMR-300 Plant Safety System Logic Basis [2]. The PSS initiates interlocks to ensure systems are aligned to allow ESF actuations to function in the modes required. The equipment receiving these interlocks is typically locked in its safe position in the modes it's required. The interlock provides an automatic position of these components to the required state if operators fail to position them prior to needing the function.

The PSS monitors plant parameters to provide protective action, including reactor trip, to prevent safety limits from being exceeded. The basis for the parameters and setpoints monitored are included in the SMR-300 Plant Safety System Logic Basis [2]. The PSS initiates a RT when required by opening reactor trip breakers. The output actuates both the undervoltage and shunt trip coils on the RTB. The RTBs are configured such that each division has two parallel breakers, where a reactor trip will occur if both breakers in either division open.

The touch screen controls are at the division level. Controls for manual initiation and reset of a RT are provided on the S-VDU of each division, and via the PCS O-VDU. Initiation from any of these locations will call for both divisions to open the RTBs.
The PSS needs four independent channels.

It is essential to create four (4) distinct types of fundamental reflectors: 1D top and bottom
reflectors, a 1D radial reflector, and a 2D MxN radial reflector. The CASMO5 input file for the 1D
reflector models closely resembles that of a non-Gad fuel assembly input file, assuming a fuel
enrichment of 4.95 wt% 235U. The key difference lies in the exclusion of the smeared spacer card
from the reflector model. However, the 1D radial reflector is specifically employed to furnish
assembly-specific information to the 2D MxN radial reflector model [21]. The CASMO5 input file
for the 2D MxN radial reflector models 1/8th of the core out to the reactor pressure vessel.

A2-2.1 Bottom and Top Reflectors
To build the input for the bottom and top reflectors, it is imperative to ascertain the thickness and
material composition—essentially, the homogenization of materials—in each reflector region or
zone. Each material is characterized by volume fractions representing specific compositions, such
as coolant, zircaloy, stainless steel, and helium. Initially, segment thickness and material
compositions are calculated, followed by the specification of input cards.

Bailer with String or Rope Commercially-available bailers will be used to obtain groundwater for use in the analysis of soil distribution coefficients for this project. Each bailer will be new and discarded following each use or dedicated to one monitoring well. Bailers will be composed of an inert, non-conductive material, such as polypropylene. Bailers will be lowered into the well using string or rope of sufficient strength to retrieve the filled bailer and resist potential breakage from any sharp edges on the well casing. The bailer string will be composed of a similar inert, non-conductive material, such as nylon or polypropylene. Any used string or rope will be discarded between wells. There are no additional requirements or specifications for bailers used for groundwater sampling for this project. Commercially-available bailers, as described above, are adequate for use under this PI.

Manual groundwater level measurements (also commonly referred to as groundwater gauging or depth-to-water measurements) are a SR activity that will be conducted in accordance with this PI. Manual groundwater level measurements will be collected from installed wells over a minimum 12-month period to determine a maximum groundwater elevation and characterize seasonal groundwater level fluctuations. Automatic water level transducers will be installed in selected wells to monitor changes in groundwater elevations to supplement the monthly manual water level measurements.

Project Field Log - Field data may be recorded in a bound field logbook or on an appropriate form/data sheet. All recorded data will be in indelible ink. All original field data sheets in a loose format will be bound and numbered at the project completion to ensure against loss. Each field log will be specific to the fieldwork conducted for the HOLTEC SMR project and labeled with a start and end date (when known). If multiple field logs are necessary, each logbook shall be assigned a unique sequential number or identifier. The BEF is the most likely flow rate to occur in the RCS loop when the plant is operating at normal full-power conditions. This operating state is the design basis point for the RCP. The TDF is the minimum flow required by the RCPs to ensure that there is margin to the departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR). The TDF accounts for SGE tube plugging, uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH greater than the TDH calculated at TDF conditions. The MDF is a conservatively high flow rate that is used as the basis for the mechanical design of the components within the RCS. The MDF accounts for uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH less than the TDH calculated MDF conditions.

entry.section_title: Groundwater and Surface Water Sample Analysis
entry.text: Groundwater samples will be submitted to the laboratory and analyzed for the parameters listed in Table 1. Samples are not to be filtered in the field unless required by the laboratory or analysis method.
ENERCON staff will maintain sample custody from the time the sample is collected until the sample is released for transportation.

A chain of custody form, provided the analytical laboratory, will be completed to document the sample collector, sample transporter(s), and sample recipient (analysis laboratory, to be determined). The sample transporter may include other ENERCON employees or freight companies. The original chain of custody form will accompany the samples throughout transportation. Samples shall be consumed at the laboratory; no sample material will be returned to ENERCON. The recipient laboratory will be requested to return the completed chain of custody form (or provide a copy) with the completed analytical results. Technical staff will keep a copy of the chain of custody that is included in the sample shipment for submittal to the HTDL (and Site Coordinator, upon request).

The TDF is the minimum flow required by the RCPs to ensure that there is margin to the departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR). The TDF accounts for SGE tube plugging, uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH greater than the TDH calculated at TDF conditions.

The MDF is a conservatively high flow rate that is used as the basis for the mechanical design of the components within the RCS. The MDF accounts for uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH less than the TDH calculated MDF conditions.

All Factory Acceptance Test Procedures and Site Acceptance Procedures shall be completed by the Supplier and submitted to the Purchaser for approval prior to testing.
The Supplier shall provide a detailed document including a submittal and delivery schedule that meets the Purchaser's project schedule requirements.

The Supplier's quality assurance program must conform to the standards specified in ASME NOA-1, Part II3.1.151. Alternatively, if another quality assurance program has been agreed upon in the purchase contract, the Supplier must adhere to that program.

All personnel who will perform QA-related inspections, tests, and examinations of the contract shall be qualified and certified as per the Supplier's Quality Assurance Program requirements. Only qualified and certified auditors shall perform audits.
Certified Material Test Reports (CMTR) or alternative such as CoC are required for all structural components in the direct load path of the RAB Crane.
The Supplier shall create and retain documented evidence to demonstrate the requirements of this specification (codes, standards, regulatory guidance etc.).
Surface coating and painting shall be performed in accordance with ASME NOG-1, Section 3000 [3.1.1] and this specification.
The RAB Crane surface coating shall be Service Level II minimum in accordance with ASME NO-1-G, Section 3000 [3.1.1].
Equipment coating colors shall be approved by the Purchaser.

All crane coating applications shall be in accordance with the job specifications and procedures and the coating manufacturer's latest published instructions to the extent referenced in the job specification and procedures. Coatings work shall be inspected by coatings inspectors qualified and certified as required by ASME NOG-1 Section 3210(c) (NACE qualification or equal). The Supplier shall provide relevant certification and reports.
The factory-applied coatings on purchased items such as gearboxes, motors, etc. may remain "as is," provided they are suitable for the environmental conditions specified.
All crane components shall be designed according to ASME NOG-1 [3.1.1].
All welding shall be in accordance with ASME NOG-1 [3.1.1] and AWS D14.1 [3.1.12] by AWS qualified personnel.
All weld quality tests and inspections (visual, non-destructive, other) shall be in accordance with AWS D14.1 [3.1.12].

All non-conformances that violate procurement documents (including drawings, procedure etc.) and that are dispositioned by the Supplier as repair/or require unusual or major rework shall be submitted to Holtec for review and approval. All base metal weld repairs apply. Standard shop manufacturing rework practices do not require review and approval by Holtec unless specified in procurement documents. Base metal weld repair is not considered standard rework practice.

The closed box section of the crane structure should be vented to supply drainage to avoid standing water in the crane structure. (Note: Sealed box girders that are designed to stand the normal atmosphere pressure are acceptable.)

Suitably located lifting lugs or eyes of adequate strength shall be furnished to facilitate erection of the major subassemblies and for removal of existing crane components. Weight and center of gravity shall be marked on major components.

All tests and inspections shall be performed in accordance with Supplier's written procedures. This specification provides the technical and quality requirements for the design and installation of a Reactor Auxiliary Building (RAB) Crane for SMR lifting operations. The intent of this specification is to provide prospective Suppliers with the information necessary to prepare proposals for construction and installation of a RAB Crane in Reactor Auxiliary Building (RAB) area.

This document provides specific design information relevant to the interfaces within the Reactor Auxiliary Building, operational requirements for the RAB Crane, specific operational features required by the Purchaser, and the major safety requirements as outlined in ASME NOG-1 [3.1.1].
The supplier/manufacturer is required to provide the RAB Crane in full compliance with ASME NOG-1 standards and all specifications outlined in this document.

The current design of Reactor Auxiliary Building layout for the SMR is not yet finalized, and therefore the operational limit requirements for the RAB Crane cannot be fully verified at this stage. For bidding purposes, some estimates have been provided to guide vendors. If, during the design or bidding process, certain travel or hoisting limits are found to be unachievable without requiring costly or complex special design solutions, vendors are encouraged to request clarification from Holtec.

5.3.1 The RAB Crane system is denoted as a Seismic Category II non-nuclear safety related with augmented quality requirements. The objective of the SMR LLC QAP TR is to assure that Holtec International's processes and activities as delineated in Table 1.1 are in accordance with governing regulations and license requirements. The program is based on the requirements set forth in the codes and standards identified in Table 1.1.2 of this document and as further described in this SMR LLC QAP TR. The SMR LLC QAP TR applies to those quality-related activities that involve the functions of safety-related structures, systems, and components (SSCs) associated with the processes and activities identified in Table 1.1.1. Holtec International established and maintains a plant-level SSC classification listing of all safety-related SSCs and non-safety related SSCs that are significant contributors to plant safety. A list or system that identifies SSCs and activities to which this program applies is maintained at Holtec International facilities. Cost and scheduling challenges must be addressed; however, they do not prevent proper implementation of the SMR LLC QAP TR.

Delegated responsibilities may be performed under a supplier's or principal contractor's QAP, provided that the supplier or principal contractor has been approved as a supplier in accordance with the SMR LLC QAP TR. Periodic audits and assessments of supplier QA programs are performed to assure compliance with the supplier's or principal contractor's QAP and that quality expectations are met. In addition, routine interfaces with the supplier's personnel provide added assurance that quality procedures are met.

Except where noted in other sections of the SMR LLC QAP TR, a grace period of 90 days may be applied to provisions that are required to be performed on a periodic basis. Annual evaluations and audits that must be performed on a triennial basis are examples where the 90-day general period could be applied. The grace period does not allow the "clock" for a particular activity to be reset forward. The "clock" for an activity is reset backwards by performing the activity early. Audit schedules are based on the month in which the audit starts.

Holtec International has established the necessary measures and governing procedures to demonstrate that items will perform satisfactorily in service. The test program includes, as appropriate, proof tests prior to installation, construction tests and preoperational tests. Test programs include criteria for determining when testing is required in order to demonstrate that performance of an item or items is in accordance with design. Tests are performed according to procedures that include, as applicable and consistent with the effect on safety: (1) instructions and prerequisites to perform the tests, (2) use of proper test equipment, (3) acceptance criteria, (4) mandatory verification points as necessary to confirm satisfactory test completion, (5) any special qualification requirements for personnel and (6) any special environmental conditions.

Test results are documented and reviewed to assure that the test requirements have been satisfied. Test records are traceable to the item(s) tested. If acceptance criteria are not met, re-testing is performed as needed to confirm acceptability following correction of the item deficiencies that caused the failure.

Test records, at a minimum and as applicable, shall identify the item tested, date of test, tester or data recorder, type of observation, results and acceptability, action taken in connection with any deviations noted, and the person evaluating the test results.

Holtec International establishes and implements provisions to assure that computer programs used in applications affecting safety are prepared, documented, verified, and tested, and used such that the expected output is obtained, and configuration control maintained. Procedures are in place to address controls for both Holtec International-generated computer programs and computer programs Holtec International-purchased.

In establishing testing requirements, Holtec International commits to compliance with NQA-1-2015, Part 1, Requirement 11 and NQA-1-2015 Part 2, Subpart 2.7 "Quality Assurance Requirements for Computer Software for Nuclear Facility Applications".

Holtec International has established the necessary measures and governing procedures to control the calibration, maintenance, and use of M&TE that are used for activities affecting quality. The provisions of such procedures cover equipment such as tools, gages, and instruments. Appropriate documentation will be maintained for M&TE to indicate the control status, when the next calibration is due, and identify any limitations on use of the M&TE. Calibration records that are traceable to the specific M&TE shall provide results of calibration.

M&TE are calibrated at prescribed intervals, or prior to use, against certified equipment having known valid relationships to nationally recognized standards. If no nationally recognized standards exist, the basis for calibration is documented.

Procedures also address requirements for control and evaluation of out of calibration conditions. A calibration is performed when the accuracy of the equipment is suspect. When measuring and test equipment is lost, damaged, or found to be out-of-calibration, the validity of previous measurement, inspection, or test results, and the acceptability of items previously inspected or tested, shall be evaluated.
In establishing provisions for control of measuring and test equipment, Holtec International commits to compliance with NQA-1-2015, Part 1, Requirement 12.

Holtec International has established the necessary measures and governing procedures to identify and control items to prevent the use of incorrect or defective items. This includes controls for consumable materials and items with limited shelf life. The identification of items is maintained from receipt and fabrication up to and including installation and use so that the item can be traced to its documentation and be related to design or other applicable specifying documents. Identification locations and methods are selected so as not to affect the function or quality of the item.
In establishing provisions for identification and control of items, Holtec International commits to compliance with NQA-1-2015, Part 1, Requirement 8.

Personnel are qualified and special processes are performed in accordance with applicable codes, standards, specifications, criteria, or other specially established requirements.
